sysd-msg-001.title: API: the contract between two pieces of software
sysd-msg-001.text: You almost never see an API, because it was not built for you. API stands for Application Programming Interface: a set of definitions and protocols for building and integrating application software. It is a software interface through which one piece of software offers a service to other pieces of software. Unlike a user interface, it works under the hood, for machine-to-machine communication. An API is sometimes called a contract: the provider sets out what it must supply, and the consumer what it must send. The calls go by several names, including subroutines, methods, requests and endpoints. A main purpose is to hide internal details and expose only the useful parts, kept consistent even if the inside later changes. Choosing the right API technology, such as {{ref:sysd-msg-002}}, {{ref:sysd-msg-004}} or {{ref:sysd-msg-005}}, is a crucial part of any system.

sysd-msg-002.title: REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs
sysd-msg-002.text:
REST is the default way to design an API, and the word has wandered a long way from its meaning. It stands for Representational State Transfer, first introduced by Roy Fielding in 2000. It is a software architectural style, created to describe and guide the design of the Web's architecture. Its constraints say how a distributed, Internet-scale hypermedia system should behave. A REST API, also called a RESTful API, conforms to those constraints, which {{ref:sysd-msg-003}} lists.

In a REST API the fundamental unit is a resource, and HTTP request methods say what to do with it. GET requests a representation of a resource. POST submits an entity and often changes state. PUT replaces the resource with the payload, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE removes it. A users resource shows the pattern. GET on /users lists all users, and POST on /users adds one. GET, PATCH and DELETE on /users/{id} read, update or delete a single user.

REST emphasizes uniform interfaces, independent deployment of components, scalable interactions and a layered architecture. That layering promotes caching, which reduces the latency users perceive, enforces security and encapsulates legacy systems. The style is simple, flexible, portable, cache-friendly and decoupled, but it can over-fetch data and need multiple round trips. A warning on vocabulary: RESTful properly means following the constraints. The term now mostly means HTTP API design and verb practices, which have little to do with REST as originally formulated.

sysd-msg-018.title: Remote procedure call: making a far-away function feel local
sysd-msg-018.text: Calling a function on another computer can look exactly like calling one in your own program. That is a remote procedure call, or RPC. The program causes a procedure to run in a different address space, commonly on another computer. The call is written as if it were a normal local call. The programmer writes essentially the same code either way. Typically it is request-response. The client sends a message with parameters, the server responds, and the client is blocked meanwhile unless it sent an asynchronous request. The illusion has limits. Remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local ones, so telling them apart matters. A caller often cannot know whether a failed remote procedure ran, though idempotent procedures are easily handled. Many incompatible technologies implement RPC, including XML-RPC, JSON-RPC and {{ref:sysd-msg-122}}. Modern frameworks such as {{ref:sysd-msg-005}} add efficient binary {{ref:sysd-msg-125}}, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming and error handling.

sysd-msg-004.title: GraphQL: asking for exactly the data you need
sysd-msg-004.text: A REST endpoint hands you whatever it was built to return. GraphQL lets the client ask for less. It is a query language and server-side runtime for APIs that gives clients exactly the data they request and no more. Through a single endpoint, the client names the exact fields it wants, nested ones included, and the server returns just those. A schema describes what clients can do. A query is a request made of fields and arguments, a mutation modifies server-side data, and a resolver is the handler that generates the response. The advantages are no over-fetching, a strongly defined schema, code generation support and optimized payloads. The costs are that complexity shifts to the server side, caching becomes hard, versioning is ambiguous and the N+1 problem appears. One source puts the complexity on the client side and warns of abusive queries if not safeguarded. GraphQL is not a full graph query language such as SPARQL: it cannot return all of an individual's ancestors in a single query.

sysd-msg-125.title: Serialization: turning data into bytes and back
sysd-msg-125.text: Copying a data structure's memory straight onto the wire does not work reliably. Byte ordering, memory layout and each language's own data representation differ across architectures, so the format must not depend on the machine. Serialization translates a data structure or object state into such a format, one that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, possibly on another computer. Rereading the bits creates a semantically identical clone of the original. This is called marshalling, and the reverse is deserialization or unmarshalling. Systems use it to send messages over networks, store data in databases and on disk, and make remote procedure calls. It has costs. The encoding is serial, so extracting one part means reconstructing the whole object. Some language serializers are also unsafe with untrusted input. Python's pickle is not secure against erroneous or malicious data, and PHP's unserialize() is often dangerous on completely untrusted data.

sysd-msg-003.title: The six constraints that make an API RESTful
sysd-msg-003.text:
REST comes down to six guiding constraints, and one of them is optional. They are uniform interface, client-server, stateless, cacheable, layered system and, optionally, code on demand. A system that applies them can be called RESTful.

Client-server separates clients from servers by a well-defined interface, with the interaction managed through HTTP. The uniform interface constraint gives one uniform way of interacting with a given server. Stateless means no client context is stored on the server between requests, so a client at rest consumes no server storage. Cacheable means every response states whether it can be cached and for how long the client may keep it. A layered system is built from several layers. A client cannot ordinarily tell whether it is connected directly to the end server or to an intermediary. Code on demand is the optional one. Servers can temporarily extend or customize a client by sending executable logic that runs in a standard {{ref:sysd-reliab-065}}.

The payoff is a set of desirable properties: performance, scalability, simplicity, modifiability, visibility, portability and reliability. Fielding also named practices that break the rules. Embedding session information in URIs violates REST because it can hurt shared caching and server scalability. HTTP cookies violate it too, because they can fall out of sync with the browser's application state. The sources differ on one point: one says an API must conform to all the constraints, code on demand included, to be RESTful.

sysd-msg-017.title: The uniform interface: one way to talk to every resource
sysd-msg-017.text: In a fully RESTful system a client needs to know only one address. The uniform interface is fundamental to any RESTful system. It gives every part one uniform way to interact, which simplifies and decouples the architecture so each part can evolve independently. It has four pieces. Resources are identified by URIs. A resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form. A client holding a representation, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state. Each message is self-descriptive, carrying enough information to say how to process it, such as a media type that names which parser to invoke. The fourth piece is {{ref:sysd-msg-123}}: after the initial URI, the client follows server-provided links, with no hard-coded knowledge of the server's structure. Because only the first identifier must be known, identifiers can change without warning, so client and server must be loosely coupled.

sysd-msg-123.title: HATEOAS: letting the server say what you can do next
sysd-msg-123.text: An overdrawn account offers one link: deposit. That small detail is HATEOAS at work. Hypermedia as the engine of application state is a REST constraint. Under it, a client discovers what it can do next from the hypermedia links the server returns. In the account example, a response offers links to deposit, withdraw, transfer or close. Once the account is overdrawn, only the deposit link remains, so the available actions vary with the resource's state. The client enters through one entry point URL, and every later request is discovered inside a response. It needs little prior knowledge of the server beyond a generic understanding of hypermedia. HTML is itself hypermedia, and formats such as HAL, JSON-LD, Siren and Collection+JSON add links to JSON or XML. The constraint decouples client and server and lets server functionality evolve independently. Fielding says the strictness of REST aims at software design on the scale of decades, and that many constraints oppose short-term efficiency.

sysd-msg-126.title: Serialization formats from compact binary to readable text
sysd-msg-126.text: Serialization formats run along a line from compact binary to human-readable text. At the compact end is Sun's External Data Representation, XDR, published in 1987: an open binary format standardized as RFC 4506. XML went the other way. It gave a human-readable text encoding, useful for objects that people read or that other systems consume regardless of language. It lost the compact byte stream, which mattered less once storage and transmission capacity grew. JSON is a lightweight plain-text alternative to XML. It is commonly used for client-server communication in web applications, is independent of JavaScript and is standardized as RFC 8259. YAML is a strict superset of JSON that adds data type tags, cyclic data structures, indentation-sensitive syntax and several forms of scalar quoting. Large scientific datasets have binary standards of their own: HDF, netCDF and GRIB. Avro, from Hadoop, serves as a format for persistent data and as a wire format, with binary and JSON encodings. Unlike {{ref:sysd-msg-006}}, it needs no code generation when a schema changes.

sysd-msg-006.title: Protocol buffers: schemas that skip the field names
sysd-msg-006.text: Protocol buffers save space by never sending a field's name. Protocol Buffers is an open-source, cross-platform data format and interface definition language for serializing structured data in a compact, forward- and backward-compatible way. It was designed to be smaller and faster than XML or JSON. Schemas and services are described in a .proto file and compiled with protoc into native language bindings. A sender or recipient invokes that generated code to produce or parse the data. A schema identifies each field by an integer, and the data carries only those numbers, which saves bandwidth and storage. The compact binary wire format is not self-describing. The text format is self-describing but loses compatibility, so it suits only human editing and debugging. {{ref:sysd-msg-005}} uses protocol buffers as its interface definition language and to encode data. The format suits small chunks of data, not exceeding a few megabytes, so it is not streamable, and it has no built-in compression.

sysd-msg-005.title: gRPC: fast, typed calls between services
sysd-msg-005.text: gRPC is said to be 5X faster than JSON, and its design explains why. It is a high-performance, open-source Remote Procedure Call framework that can run in any environment. It defines a service and the methods that can be called remotely, with their parameters and return types, using protocol buffers as the interface definition language. The client encodes a call in binary and sends it over HTTP/2. The server decodes it, invokes the application and returns an encoded result. Binary encoding and network optimizations are behind the speed. Around that core sit bidirectional streaming and flow control, cancellation and timeouts. Load balancing, tracing and health checking are pluggable. gRPC suits efficient communication between microservices, low latency and high throughput, and polyglot environments. Its disadvantages are limited browser support, a steeper learning curve, payloads that are not human readable, and being relatively new compared with REST and GraphQL. Because gRPC relies on HTTP trailers, a browser cannot be a gRPC client without a proxy.

sysd-msg-122.title: SOAP: XML envelopes for web services
sysd-msg-122.text: In financial messaging, SOAP produced messages 2-4 times larger than FIX and CDR. That weight explains much of its story. SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information in web services, usually carried over HTTP. A message is an ordinary XML document with a required Envelope and Body, an optional Header, and an optional Fault element that reports processing errors. It travels from its originator through intermediary nodes, which process the header blocks aimed at them, to the ultimate receiver. HTTP won as transport because it works well with firewalls, which normally filter distributed protocols such as GIOP/IIOP or DCOM. XML's lengthy syntax eases error detection and avoids byte-order problems but slows processing. And because SOAP is protocol-agnostic, it cannot use REST's uniform interface or caching and must reimplement them. Verbosity, slow XML parsing and no standard interaction model led services to use HTTP more directly, as REST does.

sysd-msg-014.title: API documentation: telling clients what they need to know
sysd-msg-014.text: A parameter cannot be null. A function is not thread safe. Details like these are what API documentation records. It describes what services an API offers and how to use them, and it is crucial for developing and maintaining the applications that use the API. It may include classes and methods, usage scenarios, code snippets, design rationales and contracts, but it usually omits implementation details. The catch is that it tends to be comprehensive. Writers find it hard to keep updated, and users find it hard to read carefully, which can yield bugs.

sysd-msg-012.title: API release policies: private, partner and public
sysd-msg-012.text: Not every API is meant for the whole world. A company can release one in three ways. A private API is for internal company use only. A partner API is open only to specific business partners, which lets the company exercise quality control by curating which apps have access. A public API is available for use by the public. Public does not always mean open to everybody, though: access is granted either by API tokens or by customer status validations.

sysd-msg-011.title: Web API: an API reached over HTTP
sysd-msg-011.text: A shipping company's API can be added to an eCommerce site. The site can then order shipping and show current rates, without the developer typing in the shipper's rate table. That is a web API at work. It is typically a set of specifications, such as HTTP request messages. Along with them comes a definition of the structure of the response messages, usually in XML or JSON. The term API is often used to mean web APIs, which allow communication between computers joined by the internet. The trend has run from SOAP-based web services and service-oriented architecture towards REST-style web resources and resource-oriented architecture.

sysd-msg-013.title: API versioning and deprecation: changing without breaking clients
sysd-msg-013.text: Adding a new parameter to a function call can break compatibility with the clients that make it. Once an API is public, its interface stability matters, so parts subject to change should be documented as unstable. A public API can also declare parts deprecated, making them candidates for removal or backward-incompatible change. Designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrades. GraphQL mostly avoids the problem, because it returns only the data explicitly requested. New types or fields can be added without a breaking change, and @deprecated marks parts being retired. Common practice is a versionless API, though Singh lists its versioning as ambiguous.

sysd-msg-009.title: API pagination: six ways to return a big list in pieces
sysd-msg-009.text: There are six common ways to hand back a large dataset in pieces, and they trade simplicity against speed. Offset-based pagination passes an offset and a limit, as in GET /orders?offset=0&limit=3. It is simple but inefficient for large offsets, because rows must be scanned and skipped. Page-based pagination gives a page number and a page size, as in GET /items?page=2&size=3, and has the same problem for large page numbers. Cursor-based pagination marks a position with a cursor, typically an encoded string that points to a specific record. Skipped records are not scanned, so it is efficient for large datasets, if slightly more complex. Keyset-based pagination filters by a key, as in GET /items?after_id=102&limit=3, and needs a unique, indexed key. Time-based pagination uses a timestamp or date range and misses no records when new ones are added, but needs a reliable timestamp. Hybrid pagination combines techniques, such as cursor with time-based, for the best performance and flexibility, at the price of careful design.

sysd-msg-008.title: API design best practices beyond the URL path
sysd-msg-008.text: API design is more than choosing URL paths. It means choosing resource names, identifiers and path patterns, plus HTTP header fields and rate-limiting rules within the API gateway. For a RESTful API the path structure can follow the domain model. Semantic paths make the API easier to understand, so users find the right call in the documentation. Defining only a few basic HTTP methods simplifies the design; PATCH, for example, can often be a problem for teams. Designing for idempotence in advance makes an API more robust: GET is idempotent, but POST has to be designed properly to be idempotent. Limiting the status codes in use to a defined few simplifies application development, and designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrades. For batch operations, use batch or bulk as a keyword and put it at the end of the path. A set of query rules such as pagination, sorting and filtering makes an API more flexible.

sysd-msg-019.title: RPC call sequence: from caller to server and back
sysd-msg-019.text: A remote call looks like a local one, but a lot happens in between. The caller makes a local procedure call, with parameters pushed on the stack as usual. The client stub packs the parameters into a message (marshalling) and makes a system call to send it. It is the code that stands in for the remote procedure on the caller's side. The client's operating system sends the message to the server machine, whose operating system passes the incoming packets to the server stub. The server stub unpacks the parameters (unmarshalling) and calls the server procedure. The reply traces the same steps in reverse.

sysd-msg-007.title: Choosing between REST, GraphQL and gRPC
sysd-msg-007.text:
Ask which of REST, GraphQL and gRPC is best, and the sources answer that none is. There is no silver bullet, and the right choice depends on the application's requirements and the team. The comparison runs on eight criteria: tight coupling, chattiness, performance, integration complexity, caching, built-in tooling and code generation, discoverability, and ease of versioning. Chattiness means how many separate API calls it takes to get the information needed.

REST rates low on coupling, high on chattiness and good on performance. It rates medium on complexity, great on caching, bad on code generation, good on discoverability and easy on versioning. GraphQL rates medium on coupling, low on chattiness and good on performance. It rates high on complexity, custom on caching and good on code generation. The ratings for gRPC are high on coupling, medium on chattiness and great on performance. Its complexity is low, its caching custom, its code generation great, its discoverability bad and its versioning hard.

In practice, REST suits simple, uniform interfaces between separate services and straightforward caching, though assembling related data from separate endpoints may take multiple round trips. GraphQL is good at aggregating data from several sources for rapidly evolving frontends. It can allow abusive queries if not safeguarded, and its caching is more complicated than REST's. The advice is to focus on the domain and the requirements, not the technology.

sysd-msg-015.title: GraphQL schema and type system
sysd-msg-015.text: A GraphQL service begins as a list of types. Types with fields make up the schema definition, and functions called resolvers retrieve and map the data for each field. The type system describes what data can be queried, so clients can send queries that return predictable results. The root type, Query by default, holds all queryable fields. Fields are nullable by default, a trailing exclamation mark makes a field required, and square brackets make it a list. A query is validated against the schema before the server executes it, and the result mirrors the shape of the query, typically as JSON.

sysd-msg-016.title: GraphQL operations: queries, mutations and subscriptions
sysd-msg-016.text: GraphQL does three things with data: it reads it, changes it and watches it. A query defines the exact shape of the data the client needs, and the data comes back in the same shape. A mutation creates, updates or deletes data. It generally takes variables that pass data from client to server, and it defines the shape of the data returned afterwards. A subscription sends live updates from server to client. The client defines the shape of the data it needs, and when a mutation updates the field, data goes to all subscribed clients. Real-time updates are commonly implemented using {{ref:sysd-msg-108}}.

sysd-msg-124.title: OpenAPI Specification: writing the contract first
sysd-msg-124.text: What if the contract existed before the code? In contract-first development the API contract is agreed before any code is written. Downstream developers can then mock the server and start testing right away, a shift-left testing practice. The OpenAPI Specification is a machine-readable interface definition language for describing, producing, consuming and visualizing web services. An OpenAPI Description is a formal description of an API that tools can use to generate code, documentation, test cases and more. Generated documentation keeps documentation, client libraries and source code in sync. The specification is language-agnostic and declarative, so clients can consume a service without knowing its implementation.

sysd-msg-010.title: API performance optimization: five cheap wins
sysd-msg-010.text: Five habits make an API respond faster. Pagination streams large result sets back in pieces, which improves responsiveness. Asynchronous logging sends logs to a lock-free buffer and returns at once instead of touching the disk on every call. The logs are flushed to disk periodically, which significantly reduces I/O overhead. Data caching stores frequently accessed data, so callers check the cache before querying the database, and in-memory stores such as Redis are quicker. Compressing requests and responses, for example with gzip, shortens transmission time. A connection pool reuses open database connections, avoiding the cost of opening and closing one each time.

openers.apis-rest-graphql-and-grpc: An API is the doorway through which one piece of software offers a service to another. REST draws its constraints from the architecture of the Web, GraphQL gives clients exactly the data they request and no more, and gRPC lets a program call a procedure on another computer as if it were local. Under all three lies serialization, which turns a data structure into a format that can be stored or sent and rebuilt later. The chapter also covers SOAP and the craft of documenting, versioning and changing an API without breaking the clients that depend on it.

reviews.apis-rest-graphql-and-grpc: An API is a contract, and the styles in this chapter are three ways of writing it. REST builds it from resources and uniform constraints, GraphQL from a schema that lets clients choose their fields, and gRPC from protocol buffers that make a remote call compact and fast. Each sends its data in a serialized form, from binary to text, so the choice of format shapes the size and readability of every message. None of the three is better in every case, and the best choice depends on the requirements and the team. Around the contract sits the daily craft of documentation, versioning, pagination and performance.
